conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived, and to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS—which is a short, 10-question screening that looks at mood, anxiety, and overall emotional adjustment in the first weeks and months after birth. Everything you share stays between you and our team; the goal is simply to understand how you’re doing so we can help you feel more like yourself again. I’ll ask each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?  

First, thinking back over the past seven days: have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?
I still enjoy the little things—like when the baby smiles or when I get a quiet moment with my coffee. They feel small, but they still make me happy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh—like yesterday my partner made a silly joke about diaper explosions and I cracked up. It hasn’t disappeared.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Mostly yes—like I’m still excited for our little weekend walk to the coffee shop or when my sister’s coming over to see the baby. Some days I’m too tired to feel pumped, but the interest is still there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really—if the baby’s fussy I figure it’s just what babies do, not something I messed up. I might think “maybe I could’ve tried a different swaddle,” but I don’t dwell on it or beat myself up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing when he’s napping, even though I can see his chest moving. It’s not constant—just quick little bursts a couple of times a day—but there’s no real reason for it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that rush of panic—just the normal “new-mom flutter” when I hear him cry, but it passes as soon as I check on him.
Things have been getting on top of me
Only a little—some mornings the dishes and laundry feel like a lot, but I still get through the day without feeling completely swamped.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No—once I’m actually in bed I sleep pretty well. If I’m up, it’s because the baby needs feeding, not because my mind is racing or I’m upset.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I get a bit teary when I’m overtired, but it’s quickly over and not the same as feeling truly down.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Hardly at all—maybe a couple of tears last week when I couldn’t soothe the baby right away, but it passed in minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that, overall, you're managing the early weeks of motherhood well-still laughing, looking forward to small pleasures, and maintaining a positive bond with your baby. Although you notice the occasional <sym>worry</sym> about breathing when your little one naps and some mild <sym>tearfulness</sym> when you're overtired, these moments are brief and do not dominate your days.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 6, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes recurring, unprovoked worries about baby's breathing occurring multiple times daily, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your EPDS total of 6 sits well below the 10-12 range where depression becomes probable. You endorse only low-level, situational <sym>anxiety</sym> and transient <sym>tearfulness</sym>, while the core mood symptoms required for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>-such as persistent low mood, marked anhedonia, guilt, sleep disturbance unrelated to infant care, and self-harm thoughts-are absent. Your preserved capacity for enjoyment, laughter, and daily functioning further supports a screening negative result. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum check-ups with your <med>midwife/PCP</med> and mention any mood changes at your next visit
2. Practice brief <sym>breathing exercises</sym> or grounding techniques when you notice the breathing-check worry; pair with a quick reality-check (e.g., watching baby's chest rise) to reinforce safety
3. Use a simple wind-down ritual-dim lights, no screens for 20 min before you settle-to consolidate the good sleep you already have once baby is back down
4. Share your EPDS result with your partner or support person so they can help watch for red-flag symptoms and encourage rest breaks
5. Re-screen with EPDS at your six-week postpartum appointment or sooner if you notice worsening mood, persistent worry, or any self-harm thoughts
6. If worries intensify or you feel too on-edge to sleep even when baby sleeps, arrange an earlier review with your <med>primary care provider</med> or a <med>perinatal mental-health counsellor</med>
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: New mother, ≤12 wk post-delivery  
Instrument: EPDS-10 (self-report)

Symptoms endorsed  
• Transient, situational tearfulness when overtired; resolves quickly  
• Occasional, brief intrusive worry about infant breathing (2–3×/day) without panic symptoms  
• Mild feeling that chores “pile up” some mornings; still able to complete daily tasks

Symptoms denied  
Persistent low mood, loss of enjoyment, guilt/self-blame, panic, sleep disturbance unrelated to infant needs, suicidal or self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Overall affective stability with preserved capacity for pleasure, humor, and attachment. Minimal functional impairment. Brief anxiety symptoms present but sub-threshold.

Screening significance  
Current score approx. 2–3 (well below clinical cutoff of 10–12). No indicators suggestive of major depressive episode or generalized anxiety disorder at this time.

Risk factors  
None of the following currently present: chronic sadness, anhedonia, guilt, self-harm thoughts, or impaired infant bonding.

Safety  
No self-harm ideation reported → no immediate safety concern.

Observation  
Screen negative for postpartum depression and anxiety today; routine paediatric/primary follow-up and psychosocial support education recommended.
